SECTIONS.title: Retrieval practice
ideas: Pulling an idea out of memory strengthens it more than reading it again. Every time you answer a question without looking, the memory gets easier to find next time.
Rereading feels productive because the page looks familiar, but familiarity is not the same as being able to recall it on an exam.
Good retrieval is effortful: close the book, write or say what you remember, then check. Getting it wrong first and then checking still helps you learn.
Flashcards, practice questions and explaining a topic to a friend are all retrieval practice.
pitfalls: Flipping a flashcard before you have actually tried to answer it turns retrieval back into rereading.

example.p: You have 30 minutes before a quiz on cell biology. What is the better plan: reread the chapter, or answer the end-of-chapter questions?
example.s: Answer the questions without looking, then check the ones you missed. Testing yourself builds recall; rereading mostly builds familiarity.

SECTIONS.title: Spacing and scheduling
ideas: The same amount of study spread over several days is remembered far longer than one long session the night before.
Short gaps let you forget a little, so the next review takes effort, and that effort is what makes the memory last.
A simple schedule: review new material the next day, again a few days later, then a week later.
pitfalls: Cramming can work for tomorrow's quiz, but most of it is gone a week later, right when the final needs it.

example.p: You can study 3 hours for an exam in 6 days. How should you split it?
example.s: Three or more shorter sessions on different days, for example 1 hour on day 1, day 3 and day 5, beats 3 hours on day 6.

SECTIONS.title: Interleaving and variety
ideas: Mixing different kinds of problems in one session (interleaving) is harder than doing twenty of the same kind in a row, but it teaches you to recognise which method a problem needs.
Exams mix topics, so practice that mixes topics looks more like the exam.
Varying where and how you study (writing, speaking, drawing a diagram) gives a memory more ways back in.
pitfalls: Blocked practice feels smooth, which can fool you into thinking you have mastered a topic you can only do when you know which chapter it is from.

SECTIONS.title: Notes that work
ideas: Notes in your own words beat copying slides word for word: putting an idea into your own words forces you to understand it.
The Cornell layout splits the page into notes, a column of questions and a short summary. The questions column becomes ready-made retrieval practice.
Within a day, reread your notes, fill gaps, and write two or three questions you could be asked.
pitfalls: Highlighting most of a page is not studying: it marks what to learn without learning it.

SECTIONS.title: Planning the week
ideas: Put every exam and deadline from every syllabus in one calendar at the start of the term, then plan backwards from each one.
Time blocking means giving each task a specific time slot, not just a place on a to-do list.
To beat procrastination, make the first step tiny and specific: open the problem set and do question 1.
pitfalls: Planning only for due dates leaves no time to review, so every week turns into catching up.

example.p: An essay is due in 10 days and you have an exam in 6. How do you plan?
example.s: Work backwards: block exam review on days 1, 3 and 5; outline the essay on day 2, draft on days 7 and 8, revise on day 9.

SECTIONS.title: Taking the exam
ideas: Skim the whole exam first and spend time in proportion to the points each question is worth.
Read each question twice and underline what it actually asks before answering.
If you get stuck, move on and come back: a later question often reminds you of what you need.
Some nerves are normal. Slow breathing and a quick first pass through questions you know both help settle them.
pitfalls: Changing answers on a hunch at the end. Change an answer only when you find a concrete reason.

items: Which study method builds the longest-lasting memory?
Answering practice questions without notes
Rereading the chapter
Highlighting key sentences
Copying the slides
Retrieving information from memory strengthens it; the others mostly build familiarity.
Rereading a chapter often feels effective mainly because
the material starts to look familiar
it is the most effortful method
it tests your memory
it spaces your study
Familiarity is easy to mistake for being able to recall.
You answer a flashcard wrong and then check it. This
still helps you learn
wastes the attempt
only works if you were close
makes the memory weaker
Trying first and then checking strengthens learning even after a wrong answer.
Which of these is retrieval practice?
Explaining a topic to a friend from memory
Watching the lecture again
Reading a summary
Rewriting notes neatly
Explaining from memory means pulling the idea out yourself.
You have 3 hours to study for an exam in 6 days. The best plan is
three 1-hour sessions on different days
3 hours the night before
3 hours today and none later
30 minutes on the morning of the exam
Spreading study over days (spacing) improves long-term memory.
Why does a short gap between reviews help?
Recalling after a little forgetting takes effort, which strengthens memory
You remember more by not reviewing
Gaps make the material easier
It shortens total study time
Effortful recall after a gap is what makes spacing work.
Cramming the night before mostly helps you
on the next day only
on the final exam
for the rest of the term
understand concepts deeply
Crammed material fades quickly.
A good simple review schedule is
next day, a few days later, then a week later
every hour on one day
only the night before
once at the end of term
Reviews at growing intervals keep memories alive.
Interleaving means
mixing different kinds of problems in one session
studying one topic until it is perfect
taking breaks every 10 minutes
studying with a partner
Interleaving mixes topics or problem types.
Why does blocked practice feel easier?
You already know which method every problem needs
The problems are simpler
It uses less time
It is a form of spacing
In a block, the method is given away by the chapter, so you never practise choosing it.
Interleaved practice mainly trains you to
recognise which method a problem needs
work faster on one kind of problem
memorise definitions
avoid hard problems
Mixed practice makes you choose the method, as exams do.
In Cornell notes, the narrow left column is used for
questions about the notes
the date
doodles
the instructor's name
The questions column becomes ready-made self-testing.
Why write notes in your own words?
Rephrasing forces you to understand the idea
It is faster than copying
Instructors require it
It makes notes longer
Putting ideas into your own words requires processing them.
Highlighting most of a page is
marking what to learn without learning it
a strong retrieval method
the same as spacing
the best way to review
Highlighting alone does not test or strengthen memory.
Time blocking means
giving each task a specific time slot
keeping a long to-do list
studying in big blocks of one subject
taking a break every hour
A task with a scheduled time is far more likely to get done.
The best first step against procrastination is
a tiny, specific action such as doing question 1
waiting until you feel motivated
planning the whole term first
cleaning your desk
Small concrete starts lower the barrier to begin.
Planning backwards means
starting from each deadline and scheduling the steps before it
doing the last task first
planning only for the next day
reviewing old exams first
Working back from deadlines leaves room for every step.
What should you do first when you get an exam?
Skim it and note how many points each question is worth
Start with the hardest question
Answer in strict order without looking ahead
Check the time remaining every minute
A quick skim lets you spend time where the points are.

move on and come back later
stay until you solve it
leave it blank for good
guess and never return
Later questions often jog your memory, and you protect your time.
When should you change an answer at the end?
When you find a concrete reason it is wrong
Whenever you feel unsure
Never
Always, to the second-best option
Change answers for reasons, not hunches.
